faqs.q: What is the difference between a surface and an underfloor wheel lathe?
faqs.a: A surface lathe stands at floor level and machines wheelsets that have been removed from the vehicle. An underfloor lathe works in a pit beneath the track and machines the wheelset while it stays in the vehicle.

faqs.q: Which model should I choose?
faqs.a: Start with your largest tread diameter, heaviest wheelset and daily volume. All three models take tread diameters of 750–1250 mm (depending on track gauge) and wheel widths of 75–145 mm. The YSL-08 has the shortest cycle (14–16 minutes floor to floor), the YSL-12 follows at 16–18 minutes and the single-tool-post YSL-21 at 50–60 minutes. We confirm the right model with our recommendation.

faqs.q: Can brake discs be machined?
faqs.a: Yes, on suitable configurations. The YSL-08 machines brake discs from 250 to 700 mm in diameter in the same setting as the wheels.

faqs.q: What foundation is needed?
faqs.a: A level, reinforced foundation at floor level, sized to the machine. No pit under the track is required. HYT provides the foundation drawing early in the project.

faqs.q: Should I choose a surface or a portal lathe?
faqs.a: Both machine removed wheelsets. A portal wheel lathe is built around a rigid portal frame for heavy cuts in continuous wheel-shop production. A surface lathe suits depots and overhaul shops that re-profile wheelsets and brake discs alongside other overhaul work. We recommend one or the other after reviewing your workload.

faqs.q: Does the wheelset have to be removed from the vehicle?
faqs.a: No. The YUL-08 machines the wheelset while it remains in the bogie. Brake gear, traction motors and axleboxes stay in place.

faqs.q: Can it machine wheels with flats or heavy hollow wear?
faqs.a: Yes. The machine measures each wheel first and calculates the cut needed to remove flats and restore the specified profile with the least material loss.

faqs.q: What civil works are needed?
faqs.a: A reinforced concrete pit under a straight, level section of track, with rails supported over the machine. HYT supplies the pit and foundation drawings and supervises installation.

faqs.q: Which wheel profiles can be machined?
faqs.a: Any profile specified by the operator can be stored in the CNC. Several profiles can be held for mixed fleets.

faqs.q: When should I choose a tandem machine instead?
faqs.a: If your depot handles long fleets with tight turnaround targets, a tandem lathe such as the YUL-12T machines two wheelsets of a bogie in one setting and reduces re-profiling time further.

faqs.q: How does the YUGL differ from the YUL-08?
faqs.a: Both are single-axle underfloor lathes that reprofile wheelsets in the vehicle. The YUGL is offered as the YUGL 30 (4 × 13.5 kW, tread diameters 580–1600 mm, 30 t axle load) and the YUGL 15 for urban vehicles. The YUL-08 has a 4 × 15 kW drive on individually floating rollers, tread diameters of 540–1500 mm and axle loads of 300 / 400 kN, and can also machine brake discs. Our engineers will recommend the model that suits your fleet.

faqs.q: Does the wheelset have to be removed from the vehicle?
faqs.a: No. The wheelset stays in the bogie, and brake gear, traction motors and axleboxes remain in place throughout the cycle.

faqs.q: Can the lathe exchange data with our maintenance system?
faqs.a: Data interfaces are agreed during the project. Tell us which maintenance system you use and what information you need from each cycle.

faqs.q: What civil works are needed?
faqs.a: A reinforced concrete pit under a straight, level section of track, with rails supported over the machine. HYT supplies the pit and foundation drawings and supervises installation.

faqs.q: Is there a tandem version?
faqs.a: Yes. For machining both wheelsets of a bogie in one setting, see the YUGLX and the established YUL-12T.

faqs.q: How much time does a tandem lathe save?
faqs.a: Machining both wheelsets of a bogie in one cycle reduces reprofiling time by up to 50% compared with a single underfloor machine. Actual savings depend on your vehicles and depot routine.

faqs.q: How does the machine handle different bogie wheelbases?
faqs.a: One machine is fixed and the other traverses along the pit. It is positioned to match the wheelbase of the bogie over the pit, so vehicles with different bogies can use the same installation.

faqs.q: Which tread diameters can be machined?
faqs.a: The YUL-12T covers tread diameters from 540 to 1500 mm. Wheel profiles and gauge are configured to your fleet.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the YUL-12T and the YUGLX?
faqs.a: Both are tandem underfloor lathes. The YUL-12T has a 4 × 15 kW drive per machine, a standard center distance of 1800–3100 mm and tread diameters of 540–1500 mm. On the YUGLX the movable machine runs on CNC-controlled linear guideways; it covers a wheelbase range of 1700–3200 mm and, as the YUGLX 30, tread diameters up to 1600 mm. Our engineers will recommend the model that suits your fleet.

faqs.q: Is a single machine enough for my depot?
faqs.a: If your re-profiling volume is moderate, a single YUL-08 may be sufficient. Share fleet size and re-profiling intervals and we will compare both options.

faqs.q: How does the YUGLX differ from the YUL-12T?
faqs.a: Both are tandem underfloor lathes. On the YUGLX one machine is fixed and the other moves on CNC-controlled linear guideways; it is offered as the YUGLX 30 (tread diameters 580–1600 mm, 30 t axle load) and YUGLX 15 for urban vehicles, with a wheelbase range of 1700–3200 mm. The YUL-12T has a 4 × 15 kW drive per machine, a standard center distance of 1800–3100 mm and tread diameters of 540–1500 mm. Our engineers will recommend the model that suits your fleet.

faqs.q: Why choose a tandem lathe over a single-axle machine?
faqs.a: A tandem lathe avoids moving the vehicle between the two axles of a bogie. For large fleets with frequent re-profiling, that saves time on every vehicle and frees depot capacity.

faqs.q: Which steps can be automated?
faqs.a: The scope is agreed per project. Typical candidates are positioning, measurement, profile selection and recording of results. Tell us where your operators spend most time today.

faqs.q: What civil works does a tandem lathe need?
faqs.a: A longer reinforced pit than a single machine, under a straight, level section of track. HYT provides the pit and foundation drawings and coordinates with your civil contractor.

faqs.q: Can machining data go into our maintenance system?
faqs.a: Yes, where an interface is agreed during the project. We define with your team which data is transferred and in what format.

faqs.q: When is a portal lathe better than an underfloor lathe?
faqs.a: When wheelsets are removed from the vehicle as part of your maintenance process, or when defects are so deep that heavy cuts are needed. If you want to re-profile without removing wheelsets, choose an underfloor lathe.

faqs.q: Which wheelsets does the YPL-02 accept?
faqs.a: Tread diameters from 750 to 1250 mm, wheel widths of 75–145 mm, axle lengths of 1850–2750 mm and wheelsets up to 50 kN. Diameter and axle-length limits depend on gauge.

faqs.q: Why does chip cross-section matter?
faqs.a: It describes how much material the tool can remove in one revolution. A larger cross-section means deep flats and hollow wear can be removed in fewer passes.

faqs.q: How does the YPL-02 differ from the YPL-04?
faqs.a: Both are portal lathes with roll-through handling for removed wheelsets. The YPL-02 has a 2 × 55 kW main drive for heavy cuts and completes a wheelset in 8–12 minutes. The YPL-04 drives the wheelset through six friction rollers and suits wheelsets with a mounted gearbox or external cartridge bearings. We recommend one or the other after reviewing your wheelsets and workflow.

faqs.q: Can the YPL-02 be part of an automated wheel shop?
faqs.a: Yes. It can be linked with wheelset handling and measuring stations as part of a wheel shop automation project.

faqs.q: What does 'roller type' mean?
faqs.a: It describes how the wheelset is driven: by six friction rollers, three per wheel, contacting the upper and lower tread flange areas. The rollers sit on rocker arms that adjust vertically, so contact stays consistent even on flat or oval wheels.

faqs.q: How does the YPL-04 differ from the YPL-02?
faqs.a: Both are portal lathes with roll-through handling for removed wheelsets. The YPL-04 drives the wheelset through six friction rollers (upper 2 × 37 kW, lower 2 × 18.5 kW), takes tread diameters from 650 mm and completes a wheelset in 12–16 minutes. The YPL-02 has a 2 × 55 kW main drive and a chip cross-section of 32–50 mm² for heavy cuts, with a cycle time of 8–12 minutes. We help you choose based on your wheelsets and workflow.

faqs.q: Is technical data available?
faqs.a: Yes – the main data is in the table above. Values that depend on track gauge, and the configuration for your wheelsets, are confirmed in the technical offer.

faqs.q: Do I need a pit?
faqs.a: Portal lathes machine removed wheelsets, so no pit beneath a running track is needed. Foundation requirements are provided with the offer.

faqs.q: What can be machined on the YVM-04?
faqs.a: Railway wheels and tires – plate, tread profile, rim and hub bore – in a single clamping, and similar round components. The machine has a turning diameter of 1600 mm, a table diameter of 1400 mm and a turning height of 600 mm.

faqs.q: Why machine wheels vertically rather than horizontally?
faqs.a: A wheel lying flat is easy to load, sits stable under its own weight and can be machined on profile and bore without re-mounting – useful for heavy, wide components.

faqs.q: Why is hub-bore accuracy so important?
faqs.a: The wheel is held on the axle by an interference fit. An inaccurate bore leads to rejected press-fits or an unreliable joint – see our wheel press page.

faqs.q: Where are HYT vertical turning machines in use?
faqs.a: HYT has supplied a CNC vertical turning lathe to the Sanpada EMU car shed in Mumbai and a CNC vertical turret lathe to the State Railway of Thailand in Bangkok.

faqs.q: Can the machine be used for non-railway parts?
faqs.a: Yes, for round components within its capacity. Customers in heavy engineering use vertical turning for flanges, rings and similar parts.

faqs.q: How does this machine differ from the ATL-01 axle turning lathe?
faqs.a: The YTB 04 turns and roller-burnishes the in-board and out-board bearing journals of wheelset axles. The ATL-01 carries out roughing and finish machining of complete axles between centers. Many wheel shops need both.

faqs.q: Why burnish after turning?
faqs.a: Turning leaves fine peaks on the surface. Burnishing presses them down, giving a smoother, compacted surface that supports the bearing better and resists wear and fretting.

faqs.q: Does burnishing remove material?
faqs.a: No. It is a cold-working process that displaces surface material rather than cutting it, so the diameter changes very little.

faqs.q: Which surfaces can be machined?
faqs.a: In-board and out-board journals of wheelset axles, with journal diameters of 70–320 mm and journal lengths of 110–480 mm, on axles of 1200–2750 mm (depending on track gauge) and wheelsets up to 50 kN.

faqs.q: Can the machine handle different axle types?
faqs.a: Yes. Programs are stored per axle type, and clamping is configured to the range of axles in your overhaul program.

faqs.q: How is the ATL-01 different from the Axle Journal Turning & Burnishing Lathe?
faqs.a: The ATL-01 carries out roughing and finish machining of complete railway axles between centers. The journal lathe (YTB 04) turns and roller-burnishes the in-board and out-board bearing journals of wheelset axles during overhaul.

faqs.q: Is the ATL-01 used in maintenance depots or only in production?
faqs.a: Both. The ATL-01 is built for high production requirements and is used in maintenance depots as well as production workshops. If your process also includes journal restoration on assembled wheelsets, see the journal turning and burnishing lathe.

faqs.q: Which axle types can be machined?
faqs.a: Axles for locomotives, coaches, wagons and multiple units, within the machine's capacity: 3000 mm between centers, 1.5 t load between centers and 600 mm swing over the cross slide. We check the fit against your axle drawings.

faqs.q: What happens after turning?
faqs.a: Depending on your specification, the axle goes on to surface finishing, inspection and testing, and then to the wheel press for mounting.

faqs.q: Can HYT supply a complete wheelset line?
faqs.a: Yes. Axle turning, wheel boring, pressing, measuring and balancing can be combined into one turnkey project.

faqs.q: Can one press mount and dismount wheels?
faqs.a: We configure the press for mounting, dismounting or both, according to your process and throughput.

faqs.q: Why record the press-fit curve?
faqs.a: The force–displacement curve shows whether the wheel seated correctly along the full length of the seat. Many railway specifications require it as evidence of a sound joint.

faqs.q: What press force do I need?
faqs.a: It depends on the wheel and axle design and the specified interference. Send us your drawings and specification, and we will size the press accordingly.

faqs.q: Can other components be pressed?
faqs.a: Yes. With suitable tooling, other parts fitted to axles – such as gears or brake discs – can be pressed on or off.

faqs.q: How does the press fit into an automated wheel shop?
faqs.a: It can be linked to handling equipment and measuring stations as part of wheel shop automation.

faqs.q: Which dimensions are measured?
faqs.a: Typically tread diameters, flange height and thickness and back-to-back distance. Further parameters are added to suit your maintenance or production specification.

faqs.q: Where should the station be placed?
faqs.a: Before a wheel lathe to plan the cut, after machining or pressing to confirm the result – or both. In an automated shop it sits at the decision point of the line.

faqs.q: Can measurements be shared with the wheel lathe or shop systems?
faqs.a: Yes, where interfaces are agreed during the project. We define which data is transferred and in what format.

faqs.q: How is accuracy maintained?
faqs.a: The station is verified against reference standards at commissioning and at regular intervals, which can be part of a maintenance contract.

faqs.q: Is the station part of HYT's wheel shop automation?
faqs.a: It can be supplied on its own or as part of a complete wheel shop automation solution.

faqs.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic balancing?
faqs.a: Static balancing corrects mass distribution in a single plane. Dynamic balancing measures during rotation and can correct in two planes, which also deals with the rocking effect of unbalance across a wide wheel or a wheelset.

faqs.q: What balance limits apply?
faqs.a: Limits are set by your specification or the applicable standard for the vehicle. The machine is configured to check against them.

faqs.q: How is unbalance corrected?
faqs.a: Usually by removing material at the position shown by the machine, for example by machining; in some designs by adding mass. The method follows your wheel specification.

faqs.q: Can wheelsets be balanced, or only wheels?
faqs.a: Both are possible, depending on configuration. Tell us whether you balance single wheels, wheelsets or both.

faqs.q: Does a re-profiled wheel need re-balancing?
faqs.a: Re-profiling removes material and can change the balance. Whether re-balancing is required depends on your maintenance rules.

faqs.q: Which operations does the machine perform?
faqs.a: Commutator turning and grinding, mica undercutting, deburring and polishing, turning and grinding of bearing journals, wire and tape banding, re-rolling and coil cut-off – all on one machine.

faqs.q: Why undercut the mica?
faqs.a: Mica wears more slowly than copper. If it stands level with or above the segments, brushes ride on it, which causes uneven contact, sparking and accelerated wear.

faqs.q: Is the machine relevant for three-phase AC traction motors?
faqs.a: Three-phase AC induction motors have no commutator, so commutator work does not apply. The machine is intended for fleets with DC traction motors and other commutator machines.

faqs.q: Which armature sizes can be handled?
faqs.a: Armatures up to 30 kN, 500–1600 mm long and 130–1500 mm in diameter, with commutator diameters of 120–900 mm and commutator lengths of 75–450 mm.

faqs.q: Can the machine be installed in an existing depot workshop?
faqs.a: Yes. It is designed for depot workshops; we confirm floor space, craneage and power requirements with the offer.

faqs.q: Does the train have to stop?
faqs.a: No. The train passes through at 3–5 km/h while the washing stages operate in sequence; a 24-coach rake is washed in 15 minutes or less.

faqs.q: Can wash water be recycled?
faqs.a: Yes. Wash water is recycled through an integrated effluent treatment plant (ETP), limiting fresh water use to a maximum of 60 litres per coach.

faqs.q: Which vehicles can be washed?
faqs.a: The plant is designed around the profiles of your vehicles. Tell us every vehicle type that will pass through it, including any planned additions to the fleet.

faqs.q: What maintenance does the plant need?
faqs.a: Brushes, nozzles, pumps and dosing equipment need routine checks and replacement. These can be covered by a maintenance contract.

faqs.q: Can the plant be added to an existing depot?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, if a suitable straight section of track and utility connections are available. We assess this during the site survey.

faqs.q: What is a rail cum road vehicle?
faqs.a: A shunter that drives on roads and runs on rails, changing between the two modes in about two minutes. In shunting mode it couples to rolling stock and moves it along the track.

faqs.q: How many vehicles can it move?
faqs.a: The KRE 15 RCRV moves up to 135 t of locomotives or other rolling stock on gradients up to 2.5 ‰, with a tractive effort of up to 15 kN. We check this against your heaviest regular movement and your depot gradients.

faqs.q: What infrastructure does it need?
faqs.a: A point where the vehicle can drive on to the track – typically a paved section level with the rails. We assess your depot layout during the inquiry.

faqs.q: Which couplers can it use?
faqs.a: The coupling system is matched to your rolling stock. Tell us which coupler and brake types your vehicles use.

faqs.q: Who can operate it?
faqs.a: Trained depot staff. Operator training is part of commissioning, and refresher training is available.

faqs.q: What does HYT's exclusive distribution mean for me?
faqs.a: HYT is the exclusive distributor of SKC Gleittechnik products in India, so inquiries, quotations, supply and support in India run through HYT.

faqs.q: Where can I see the product range?
faqs.a: Contact us with your application and we will send the relevant product information and a recommendation.

faqs.q: Can HYT advise on the right product?
faqs.a: Yes. Our engineers review the application, consult SKC where needed and recommend a solution.

faqs.q: Can SKC products be used when reconditioning older machines?
faqs.a: Reconditioning worn slideways is a typical opportunity. We assess the machine and advise whether sliding technology is suitable.

faqs.q: Do you supply outside India?
faqs.a: HYT's exclusive distribution covers India. Customers in other countries can contact us and we will advise on the right channel.

faqs.q: Can a wheel shop be modernized while it keeps working?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. We plan the work in phases, so existing machines keep running while new stations are installed alongside or in their place.

faqs.q: Should we re-profile on a surface or a portal wheel lathe?
faqs.a: Both machine removed wheelsets. The choice depends on your wheelset types, typical defect depth and the flow; see the surface and portal wheel lathe pages.

faqs.q: Does the wheel shop also need an underfloor wheel lathe?
faqs.a: An underfloor wheel lathe re-profiles wheels without removing the wheelset, so it belongs in the depot rather than the overhaul shop. Many operators use both: underfloor lathes for routine re-profiling, the wheel shop for wheelsets that come out of the vehicle anyway. See Railway Maintenance Depots.

faqs.q: Can we keep existing machines from other makers?
faqs.a: Where they are in good condition, yes. We include them in the layout and define their interfaces, so the shop works as one process.

faqs.q: Can automation be added to an existing wheel shop?
faqs.a: Yes. Automation is usually introduced in stages: first the machines and their data are connected, then handling is added as throughput grows. Each stage is planned so the shop keeps producing.

faqs.q: How are wheelset records kept?
faqs.a: Measuring, machining, pressing and balancing results are recorded against each wheelset's identity. The data format and transfer to your own systems are agreed with your quality and IT teams during engineering.

faqs.q: Single or tandem underfloor wheel lathe?
faqs.a: A tandem underfloor wheel lathe re-profiles both wheelsets of a bogie in one setting, which shortens each visit for fleets with many axles. A single machine needs a shorter pit and suits lower volumes. We size the choice against your fleet and maintenance plan.

faqs.q: Can new equipment be added to a depot that is already in use?
faqs.a: Yes. Lathe pits and washing plants are usually built on roads that can be taken out of use for a period, while the rest of the depot keeps working. We sequence the work with your operations team.

faqs.q: Does a car shed need its own capacity for machining loose wheels?
faqs.a: Some do. HYT supplied a CNC vertical turning lathe to the Sanpada EMU car shed in Mumbai, giving the shed in-house wheel machining capacity – see Executed Projects.

faqs.q: Can a Rail cum Road Vehicle replace a shunting locomotive?
faqs.a: For many depot moves, yes. It couples to rolling stock on the rails and drives on the road between tracks, so one vehicle can serve several roads. Hauling capacity, coupling and brakes are matched to your vehicles.

faqs.q: Does HYT supply bogie frames or car-body equipment?
faqs.a: No. HYT's scope covers the wheel and axle shop: machining, pressing, measuring and balancing of wheelsets, plus the handling and integration within that shop. Bogie and car-body production remain with the manufacturer and its other suppliers.

faqs.q: Can the shop serve several vehicle projects at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Machines are specified for the range of wheel and axle designs you expect, and part programs and fixtures are prepared for each variant, so changeovers become routine.

faqs.q: Can we start small and expand later?
faqs.a: Yes. The layout can reserve space and utilities for additional machines, so capacity grows with your order book without rebuilding the shop. A Rail cum Road Vehicle (Shunter) can also be added for moving finished vehicles around the factory yard.

faqs.q: How is the shop linked to our quality system?
faqs.a: Measurement, pressing and balancing results are recorded against each wheelset's identity. We agree the data format and transfer method with your quality and IT teams during engineering. For connected handling and data, see wheel shop automation.

faqs.q: How does a wheelset plant differ from a wheel shop?
faqs.a: A wheelset plant produces new wheelsets from new wheels and axles. A wheel shop overhauls wheelsets that are already in service – see Wheel Shops.

faqs.q: How is traceability achieved?
faqs.a: Each wheel and axle is identified on arrival. Its measurements, the pairing used at pressing, the force–travel record and the balancing and final inspection results are stored against that identity, so a wheelset's history can be retrieved at any time.

faqs.q: Can mounted wheelsets be finish-profiled in the plant?
faqs.a: Some specifications call for the tread profile to be finished after mounting, so that both wheels run true to the axle. A CNC Surface Wheel Lathe can be included in the line for this purpose.

faqs.q: Can one plant produce to different customer standards?
faqs.a: Yes. Machine ranges, tooling, press programs and inspection limits are specified for the full product range during engineering, and each wheelset is processed against the requirements of its order.

faqs.q: Why use vertical turning machines for railway wheels?
faqs.a: The wheel lies flat on a rotary table, which makes heavy wheels easy to load and keeps them stable under cutting load. Tread, flange, faces and bore are all reachable from above. See the CNC Vertical Turning & Boring Machine YVM-04.

faqs.q: How many machines does a wheel line need?
faqs.a: It depends on wheel size, forging allowance, required output and shift pattern. We calculate cycle times for your wheels and propose the number of stations and how the operations are split between them.

faqs.q: Can the line also machine tires?
faqs.a: Yes, where your fleet uses tyred wheels. The vertical turning and boring machine also handles tires and other round wheelset components, and the line layout allows for them if specified.

faqs.q: Has HYT supplied vertical turning machines for railway wheels?
faqs.a: Yes. HYT supplied a CNC vertical turning lathe to the Sanpada EMU car shed in Mumbai and a CNC vertical turret lathe to the State Railway of Thailand in Bangkok. Details are on Executed Projects.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the ATL-01 and the journal turning and burnishing lathe?
faqs.a: The ATL-01 is a production machine that turns a complete axle from a raw or forged blank. The journal turning and burnishing lathe is an overhaul machine that restores and burnishes the journals of axles already in service. A line for new axles is built around the first; an overhaul line around the second.

faqs.q: Why burnish journals after turning?
faqs.a: Hardened rollers press down the peaks left by the turning tool and leave a smooth, compacted surface for the bearing. Burnishing is a cold-working process and produces no chips.

faqs.q: Can one line handle both new and overhaul axles?
faqs.a: Yes, if your facility needs both. The two streams use different machines but can share receipt, handling, measurement and storage, which keeps the building compact.

faqs.q: Is non-destructive testing of axles part of the line?
faqs.a: Ultrasonic and magnetic particle testing are normally carried out by the owner's inspection staff to the railway's own procedures. We plan the space for testing and the flow of axles to and from it as part of the layout.

faqs.q: How early should we involve HYT?
faqs.a: As soon as the machine is ordered – ideally while the depot layout is still being finalised. Pit and foundation drawings influence civil design and schedule, so early agreement saves time later.

faqs.q: Who carries out the civil works?
faqs.a: Normally your civil contractor, working to HYT drawings. We check the interface points before the machine arrives. In a turnkey project, civil works can be included in HYT's scope.

faqs.q: How long does commissioning take?
faqs.a: It depends on the machine type, site readiness and the availability of trial wheelsets. We share a realistic schedule with the offer and update it after the site readiness check.

faqs.q: Is operator training part of commissioning?
faqs.a: Yes. Initial training for operators and maintenance staff is delivered during commissioning. Extended or refresher programs are available through our Training service.

faqs.q: What happens after handover?
faqs.a: Your machine enters its warranty period. Many customers then continue with an Annual Maintenance Contract or a Comprehensive Maintenance Contract.

faqs.q: We have operators but no specialist maintenance staff.
faqs.a: An AMC gives you scheduled preventive visits and breakdown attendance. If you also want spare parts covered within a fixed annual budget, choose a CMC.

faqs.q: We are opening a new depot and have no trained lathe team.
faqs.a: An O&M contract lets HYT operate and maintain the machine. If your maintenance department will look after the machine, an Operation Contract covers the operators only.

faqs.q: Our machine is lightly used and our own team maintains it.
faqs.a: A call-based Service Contract gives you agreed rates for visits when you need them, and Spare Parts & Support keeps genuine parts within reach.

faqs.q: Can contracts be combined or changed later?
faqs.a: Yes. Many customers start with an O&M contract while training their own staff, then move to a CMC or AMC. We review the scope with you at each renewal.

faqs.q: How is O&M different from an Operation Contract?
faqs.a: An O&M contract covers both operation and maintenance. An Operation Contract provides operators only; maintenance stays with your team or a separate AMC or CMC.

faqs.q: Do our own staff need to be present?
faqs.a: Your depot remains in charge of rolling stock movements, safety permits and the maintenance plan. A nominated supervisor on your side keeps coordination simple.

faqs.q: Can our staff be trained to take over later?
faqs.a: Yes. An O&M contract can include structured training so that your team gradually takes over operation, with HYT continuing under an AMC or CMC.

faqs.q: How is the contract priced?
faqs.a: Usually as a periodic fee based on shifts, workload and the agreed scope. We quote after understanding your fleet and depot routine.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an AMC and a CMC?
faqs.a: An AMC covers labor for preventive visits and breakdown attendance. A CMC adds the spare parts listed in the contract, so your annual maintenance cost is fixed.

faqs.q: How many preventive visits are included?
faqs.a: The number is agreed with you, based on machine type, utilization and operating conditions. It is stated in the contract.

faqs.q: Can we take an AMC for an older machine?
faqs.a: Yes, after a condition inspection. If the machine needs repairs first, we will quote those separately – see Repair.

faqs.q: What response time can we expect for a breakdown?
faqs.a: Response commitments are written into each contract, based on the machine's location and how critical it is to your fleet. We agree them with you before the contract starts, so there is no ambiguity when a call comes in.

faqs.q: How do we report a breakdown?
faqs.a: Call the toll-free service line 1800 2100 456 or email us with the machine serial number and a description of the fault. See After-Sales Service Network.

faqs.q: Which spare parts are covered?
faqs.a: The contract includes a schedule of covered parts, agreed after a condition inspection of your machine. Consumables are normally excluded.

faqs.q: Can an older machine be placed under a CMC?
faqs.a: Usually yes, after an inspection. Any repairs needed to bring the machine to an acceptable baseline condition are quoted separately before the CMC starts.

faqs.q: How is the annual fee set?
faqs.a: After inspecting the machine, we consider its age, condition, utilization and the parts schedule you choose. The fee is fixed for the contract year, and the scope is reviewed with you at each renewal.

faqs.q: Who operates the machine under a CMC?
faqs.a: Your own operators. If you want HYT to operate the machine as well, see Operation & Maintenance (O&M).

faqs.q: What happens if a part is damaged by an accident?
faqs.a: Accidental damage is outside the CMC scope. We assess the damage, quote the repair and, once it is complete, the machine continues under the CMC.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if the machine breaks down?
faqs.a: Your maintenance team, or HYT if you also hold an AMC or CMC. Our operators will report the fault and support diagnosis with what they observed.

faqs.q: Can an Operation Contract help us train our own operators?
faqs.a: Yes. Your staff can work alongside HYT operators and attend formal training, so they can take over when the contract ends.

faqs.q: How is the contract priced?
faqs.a: Normally as a periodic fee based on the number of operators and shifts. We quote after understanding your workload.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum number of visits?
faqs.a: No. The contract fixes the rates for an agreed period; you pay only for the visits you call for.

faqs.q: Can we move to an AMC or CMC later?
faqs.a: Yes. If your call volume grows or you want scheduled preventive care, we can convert the agreement to an AMC or CMC at any time.

faqs.q: Are spare parts available under a Service Contract?
faqs.a: Yes, quoted separately for each requirement. See Spare Parts & Support.

faqs.q: Can you supply parts for older machines?
faqs.a: Yes, wherever possible. If an original component is no longer made, we propose an equivalent or a retro-fitment of the affected system.

faqs.q: Which spares should we hold on site?
faqs.a: Ask for the recommended spares list for your machine. It ranks parts by how critical they are and how long they take to source.

faqs.q: Are spare parts included in maintenance contracts?
faqs.a: They are included in a CMC, as listed in the contract. Under an AMC, parts are quoted separately.

faqs.q: How quickly can a part be delivered?
faqs.a: It depends on the part. Some items are held in stock; others are manufactured or sourced to order. The quotation states the delivery time, and if your machine is stopped, tell us so that we can prioritize.

faqs.q: Can you fit the parts for us?
faqs.a: Yes. Our engineers can attend on site under a Service Contract or as a one-off visit.

faqs.q: Retrofit or new machine – how do we decide?
faqs.a: If the structure and geometry are sound, a retrofit usually costs less and avoids civil works. If the structure is worn or your requirements have changed significantly, a new machine may be better. Our assessment sets out both options.

faqs.q: How long will the machine be out of service?
faqs.a: That depends on the scope. We plan engineering and procurement before the shutdown so that the machine is down only for installation and re-commissioning.

faqs.q: Will our operators need retraining?
faqs.a: Yes, on the new control and any new functions. Training is part of every retro-fitment project.

faqs.q: Can a retrofit add new wheel profiles?
faqs.a: Yes. New profiles for changed fleets can be added to the CNC as part of the upgrade.

faqs.q: Do you repair machines from other manufacturers?
faqs.a: Our expertise is in HYT machines, whose designs and records we hold. For other makes, send us the details and we will tell you honestly whether we can help.

faqs.q: Do we need a maintenance contract to get a repair?
faqs.a: No. Repairs are available to all HYT customers. A Service Contract fixes the rates in advance and speeds up approvals.

faqs.q: Can repairs be done on site?
faqs.a: Most repairs are carried out on site. Where an assembly needs machining or a full rebuild, it may be brought to our works in Pune.

faqs.q: What if the original parts are no longer available?
faqs.a: We propose an equivalent part or a targeted retro-fitment of the affected system.

faqs.q: What is an SPM?
faqs.a: A special purpose machine – a machine tool designed for a specific task, such as re-profiling railway wheels, pressing wheels on to axles or turning axle journals.

faqs.q: Can you relocate an underfloor wheel lathe?
faqs.a: Yes. Underfloor lathes need a new pit at the destination, so civil works must be planned early. We supply the pit drawings and check the pit before the machine is moved.

faqs.q: How long will the machine be out of service?
faqs.a: It depends on the machine, the distance and how ready the new site is. Preparing the new foundation or pit before dismantling begins is the most effective way to shorten the move, and we plan the schedule around it.

faqs.q: Who arranges transport?
faqs.a: This is agreed per project. HYT can plan and manage the full move, or work with your nominated logistics contractor.

faqs.q: Will the warranty or maintenance contract continue?
faqs.a: Contract terms are reviewed as part of the relocation. After successful re-commissioning, an AMC or CMC can continue at the new site.

faqs.q: How is wet leasing different from O&M?
faqs.a: Under an O&M contract, you own the machine and HYT runs and maintains it. With Machine as a Service, HYT also provides the machine.

faqs.q: Who prepares the pit or foundation?
faqs.a: This is agreed per project. HYT supplies the drawings and checks the works; the civil construction is usually arranged by the customer.

faqs.q: Which machines are available?
faqs.a: The machine is selected for your fleet and site, typically an underfloor wheel lathe. Talk to us about your requirement.

faqs.q: Is training included with a new machine?
faqs.a: Yes. Initial training for operators and maintainers is part of installation and commissioning.

faqs.q: Can you train staff on a machine that is several years old?
faqs.a: Yes. We tailor the content to the machine's configuration and control system.

faqs.q: In which language is training delivered?
faqs.a: Please tell us your preferred language when you inquire, and we will confirm what we can offer.

faqs.q: Should a railway shed choose an underfloor or a surface wheel lathe?
faqs.a: An underfloor lathe re-profiles wheels without removing the wheelset and is the right choice where vehicles must return to service quickly. A surface wheel lathe suits sheds that need a flexible machine without a deep pit. We can advise on the best option for your fleet and site.

faqs.q: Can one machine handle locomotives, coaches and wagons?
faqs.a: Yes. With suitable adaptors and stored wheel profiles, one machine can serve a mixed fleet. Axle load, wheel diameter range and bogie design are confirmed during the technical study.

faqs.q: Can you upgrade our existing wheel lathes?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Retro-fitment with a new CNC system, drives and measuring equipment can restore accuracy and reliability at lower cost than a new machine.

faqs.q: Do you support broad, standard and meter gauge?
faqs.a: Our wheel lathes are configured to the customer's track gauge and wheel profiles. Gauge-dependent values are confirmed in the technical offer.

faqs.q: When does a metro depot need a tandem wheel lathe?
faqs.a: When fleets are large and maintenance windows short. A tandem lathe machines two wheelsets of a bogie at once; HYT's YUL-12T reduces re-profiling time compared with a single machine.

faqs.q: Can the lathe machine brake discs as well as wheels?
faqs.a: Brake-disc machining is available on suitable configurations. We confirm it during the technical study of your vehicles.

faqs.q: How is the machine integrated into a new depot?
faqs.a: We supply pit, foundation and interface drawings early, coordinate with the depot designer and civil contractor, and commission the lathe on your own trains.

faqs.q: Can HYT operate the machine for us?
faqs.a: Yes. Under an operation and maintenance arrangement our crew runs and maintains the machine, so you can focus on running trains.

faqs.q: Can HYT supply a complete wheel shop rather than single machines?
faqs.a: Yes. We plan the process flow, select and link the machines, add handling and data systems and commission the line. See Wheel Shops and Turnkey Projects.

faqs.q: Can the machines handle different wheel sizes and gauges?
faqs.a: Our machines are configured to the range of wheels and axles you produce. Size ranges are confirmed in the technical offer for your program.

faqs.q: Is the production data recorded?
faqs.a: Data recording for measuring stations and wheel presses is defined with you in the technical offer, to support traceability and customer inspection.

faqs.q: Can HYT machines handle heavy military wagons?
faqs.a: Our wheel lathes are configured to the wheel diameters, gauges and axle loads specified by the customer. Requirements for heavy-duty wagons are reviewed in the technical study.

faqs.q: Can HYT work under confidentiality and security requirements?
faqs.a: Yes. We handle drawings, site information and project data according to the confidentiality terms of the contract and the rules of the site.

faqs.q: Is training and long-term support available?
faqs.a: Yes. We train operators and maintainers on site and offer maintenance contracts and spare parts supply for the machine's working life.

faqs.q: Can HYT vertical turning lathes machine non-railway components?
faqs.a: Our vertical turning and boring machines are designed for heavy rotating parts. Share your component drawings and we will confirm suitability and capacity.

faqs.q: We run an internal rail fleet. Do we need a full wheel shop?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A surface wheel lathe or portal wheel lathe can give a captive fleet its own re-profiling capacity without the investment of a complete wheel shop.

faqs.q: Can you relocate an existing machine to a new plant?
faqs.a: Yes. Our shifting service covers dismantling, transport, reinstallation and recommissioning.

faqs.q: How often should wheels be re-profiled?
faqs.a: There is no single interval. It depends on the vehicle, its duty, the route, the braking system and the operator's limits. Most operators re-profile on condition, using regular measurements, rather than at fixed mileages.

faqs.q: What is the difference between re-profiling and replacing a wheel?
faqs.a: Re-profiling machines the existing wheel back to its specified tread and flange shape. Replacement becomes necessary when the wheel or tire reaches its condemning diameter or has damage that cannot be machined away safely.

faqs.q: Why does a thin flange cost so much diameter?
faqs.a: The flange cannot be built up; its shape can only be restored by cutting the tread down until a full-thickness flange stands proud again. A little flange wear can therefore mean a much larger diameter loss.

faqs.q: Can wheels with flats be machined without removing the wheelset?
faqs.a: Yes. An underfloor wheel lathe machines wheels in the vehicle and can remove flats and restore the profile in the same cycle.

faqs.q: Do both wheels on an axle need to be machined together?
faqs.a: Yes, in practice. The two wheels on an axle must stay within a tight diameter tolerance of each other for the wheelset to steer correctly. Underfloor, portal and surface lathes machine both wheels in one setting.

faqs.q: When is a tandem underfloor lathe worth it?
faqs.a: When the depot handles long or high-frequency fleets and the time each train spends on the lathe is critical. A tandem lathe machines both wheelsets of a bogie in one setting.

faqs.q: Can brake discs be machined on a wheel lathe?
faqs.a: On suitable configurations, yes. Axle-mounted brake discs can be machined on some surface lathes and on underfloor lathes specified with that option. Confirm the requirement at the inquiry stage.

faqs.q: How long does it take to plan and install an underfloor lathe?
faqs.a: It depends mainly on the civil works. Pit design should start early in the depot design, as the pit and track are fixed once built. Ask us for foundation drawings at the planning stage.

faqs.q: What information do you need to recommend a machine?
faqs.a: Vehicle types and fleet size, wheel diameter range, wheel profiles, track gauge, axle loads, expected wheelsets per shift and a sketch of the depot or workshop layout.

faqs.q: Can an older wheel lathe be modernized?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A sound machine structure can be given a new CNC system, drives and measuring equipment. See retro-fitment and upgradation.

faqs.q: Do you publish job vacancies?
faqs.a: No. We accept open applications throughout the year and contact candidates whose profiles match the roles we need to fill.

faqs.q: Can graduates and interns apply?
faqs.a: Yes. Choose "Internship / graduate trainee" in the form and tell us about your studies, projects and interests.

faqs.q: Where are the jobs located?
faqs.a: Most roles are based at our Pune campus and works. Service and project roles include travel to customer sites in India and abroad.

faqs.q: What should I include in my application?
faqs.a: A current CV in PDF format, the area you are interested in, your total experience and – if you like – a short note on what you want to achieve.

faqs.q: How will I hear back?
faqs.a: Our HR team contacts shortlisted candidates by phone or email. If there is no suitable opening right now, we may keep your profile for future roles.
